name: Western Lalu
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Yang, Cathryn. 2010. Lalo regional varieties: phylogeny, dialectometry and sociolinguistics. PhD thesis, La Trobe University.
earlier_scan.note: Yang's phonological/dialect work covers Western Lalu (tonal Loloish)

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2007. Change Request 2007-085: rename 'Yi, Western Lalu' to 'Lalu, Western' [ywl] (adopted 2008-01-14)
Yang, Cathryn. 2015. Lalo dialects across time and space: subgrouping, dialectometry, and intelligibility. Asia-Pacific Linguistics A-PL 22. Canberra: ANU. 260 pp. hdl 1885/95391
sources.note: Sec. 3.5 'Western Lalo: Yilu (W-YL)' pp. 50-52 and 3.5.1-3.5.3 pp. 52-54 (same text as the thesis), sec. 5.3.3 acoustic tone analysis of W-YL, W-SZP, W-DT: silent on word stress; only tone, tone sandhi and phrase-final tone allophony ([55] > [53] phrase-finally).

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2011. Change Request 2011-095 (submitted by Cathryn Yang, SIL EAG): split [ywl] into Yangliu Lalo and Xuzhang Lalo; rejected 2012-03-28
sources.note: Intelligibility and identity only; nothing on phonology or stress.

sources.citation: Yang, Cathryn. 2010. Lalo regional varieties: phylogeny, dialectometry, and sociolinguistics. PhD dissertation, La Trobe University, Bundoora. 447 pp. doi:10.26181/21844209.v1 (La Trobe OPAL/figshare, open download)
sources.note: Sec. 3.5 'Western Lalo: W-YL' pp. 79-83 and 3.5.1-3.5.3 (W-DT, W-SZP, W-SLZ) pp. 83-84: syllable template (C)VT / NT, 29 initials, 15 rhymes, 5 tones (44, 24, 21, 33, 55[53 phrase-final]) with tone sandhi, harsh phonation lost; nothing on word stress. In the whole thesis 'stress(ed)' occurs only in the Central (CW-QY) sketch p. 64 ('Following a stressed syllable, the syllabic nasal loses its syllabicity...') and in a citation of Esling 2006. p. 3: Lalo is 'omnisyllabic' (after Matisoff 1989), 'almost every syllable is assigned a lexical tone'.

sources.citation: Yang, Cathryn. 2010. Tone change in Lalo. In Y. Treis & R. De Busser (eds), Selected papers from the 2009 Conference of the Australian Linguistic Society. 26 pp.; and Yang, Cathryn. 2012. Classifying Lalo languages: subgrouping, phonetic distance, and intelligibility. LTBA 35(2): 113-137
sources.note: Tone change and classification; silent on stress (per the dong1286 audit notes).

sources.citation: Yang, Cathryn. 2009. Regional variation in Lalo: beyond east and west. La Trobe Papers in Linguistics 12. 35 pp. doi:10.26181/22202464.v1
sources.note: Subgrouping/dialectometry; silent on stress (per the xuzh1234 and xish1235 audit notes; not re-read here).

sources.citation: Yang, Cathryn, James N. Stanford & Zhengyu Yang. 2015. A sociotonetic study of Lalo tone split in progress. Asia-Pacific Language Variation 1(1): 52-77.

sources.note: Acoustic study of a Lalo tone split (the Tone *1 split is a Western Lalo innovation per Yang 2015 sec. 5.3), so possibly the only instrumental prosodic study of a Western Lalo variety; might mention intensity/duration prominence. Variety not confirmed from the record.

sources.note: Chinese comparative treatment with a Western-Yi (Weishan) phonological sketch; Chinese Yi descriptions occasionally note whether zhongyin (stress) is distinctive.

sources.citation: Björverud, Susanna. 1998. A grammar of Lalo. PhD dissertation, Lund University (Department of East Asian Languages). Longjie township, Weishan = West Mountain Central Lalo.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.access_detail: HathiTrust digitized, search-only (in copyright); interlibrary loan
sources.note: The only full reference grammar of any Lalo variety; its phonology chapter is the most likely place for an explicit statement on stress in Lalo (even if only that it is non-contrastive). Describes Central Lalo (xish1235), not Western Lalo, so it could serve only as a sister-variety statement with an identity note.
